```{=html}
<div class="lx-card ckm-intro">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">How this checkpoint works · about 240 minutes, no hints</p>
<ol class="ckm-parts">
<li><b>A · The brief</b> (about 120 min). Choose a variant. <b>Model:</b> formulate the water brief as a <span class="lx-term" data-term="linear-program">linear program</span>, solve it and read the solution. <b>Empirical:</b> analyse a real year of grid data.</li>
<li><b>B · The planted defect</b> (about 60 min). Find the one defect in a supplied model, say which check shows it, fix it and solve again.</li>
<li><b>C · Validation</b> (about 45 min). Check one of your results against an independent reference: hand calculations (model) or a published figure (empirical).</li>
<li><b>Submit</b> (about 15 min). Enter your results in the eleven tasks below. The worked formulations and code open when you submit task 11.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">How it is marked, before you start</p>
<ul class="ckm-rules">
<li><b>Proficient:</b> at least 6 of the 9 auto-marked tasks right on the first try, including the defect's line (task 6), plus 3 of the 4 points of task 1 and 2 of the 3 of task 11, which you tick yourself.</li>
<li><b>Strong:</b> 8 of 9 on the first try, the defect's line among them, and every written point.</li>
<li><b>Tolerances:</b> each number task says how close counts as right.</li>
<li><b>Opening solutions early:</b> a task whose solution you open before answering counts as not right. Opening the full worked solutions before task 11 makes the attempt practice, with no level.</li>
</ul>
<p class="ckm-dl"><a class="lx-btn small" href="notebooks/ck-m-start.ipynb" download>Starter notebook (.ipynb)</a> <a class="lx-btn small ghost" href="../assets/learn/data/town_year.json" download>Dataset: town_year.json</a> <a class="lx-btn small ghost" href="../assets/learn/data/ck-m-unseen-problem-briefs.json" download>Briefs and model data (JSON, no answers)</a></p>

<div class="lx-row2 ckm-briefs">
<div class="lx-card ckm-brief" id="ckm-brief-model">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Model variant · the brief</p>
<h3>Pumping water for the least electricity cost</h3>
<!-- ckm-brief-model:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p>Prairie Town's water utility pumps groundwater into a water tower, and the town draws its water from the tower. Find tomorrow's pumping schedule that meets the town's water use at the least electricity cost for the day. <span class="lx-hint">All numbers in this brief are illustrative.</span></p>
<ul class="ckm-facts"><li><b>Water use:</b> forecast for each hour of tomorrow, in the table below (m³)</li><li><b>Pumps:</b> lift up to 900 m³ an hour and use 0.5 kWh of electricity per m³ pumped</li><li><b>Tower:</b> holds 800 to 4,000 m³; 2,000 m³ at the start of the day, and at least as much at the end</li><li><b>Energy price:</b> the rural electric co-op's time-of-use price: $0.06 per kWh from 22:00 to 06:00, $0.20 from 16:00 to 21:00, $0.10 otherwise</li><li><b>Demand charge:</b> $0.40 for each kW of the day's highest hourly draw</li></ul>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Hourly water use and price</summary><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Hour</th><th scope="col">Water use (m³)</th><th scope="col">Price ($/kWh)</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>00:00</td><td>180</td><td>0.06</td></tr><tr><td>01:00</td><td>160</td><td>0.06</td></tr><tr><td>02:00</td><td>150</td><td>0.06</td></tr><tr><td>03:00</td><td>150</td><td>0.06</td></tr><tr><td>04:00</td><td>170</td><td>0.06</td></tr><tr><td>05:00</td><td>250</td><td>0.06</td></tr><tr><td>06:00</td><td>420</td><td>0.10</td></tr><tr><td>07:00</td><td>610</td><td>0.10</td></tr><tr><td>08:00</td><td>640</td><td>0.10</td></tr><tr><td>09:00</td><td>560</td><td>0.10</td></tr><tr><td>10:00</td><td>480</td><td>0.10</td></tr><tr><td>11:00</td><td>450</td><td>0.10</td></tr><tr><td>12:00</td><td>440</td><td>0.10</td></tr><tr><td>13:00</td><td>430</td><td>0.10</td></tr><tr><td>14:00</td><td>420</td><td>0.10</td></tr><tr><td>15:00</td><td>430</td><td>0.10</td></tr><tr><td>16:00</td><td>470</td><td>0.20</td></tr><tr><td>17:00</td><td>560</td><td>0.20</td></tr><tr><td>18:00</td><td>640</td><td>0.20</td></tr><tr><td>19:00</td><td>650</td><td>0.20</td></tr><tr><td>20:00</td><td>560</td><td>0.20</td></tr><tr><td>21:00</td><td>430</td><td>0.10</td></tr><tr><td>22:00</td><td>320</td><td>0.06</td></tr><tr><td>23:00</td><td>230</td><td>0.06</td></tr></tbody></table></div></details>
<!-- ckm-brief-model:end -->
</div>
<div class="lx-card ckm-brief" id="ckm-brief-empirical">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Empirical variant · the brief</p>
<h3>What can the town count on at its peaks?</h3>
<!-- ckm-brief-empirical:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p>Prairie Town's planners want to know how far its wind and solar farms can be counted on when the town needs power most. Report what the town can and cannot count on, and how far your results depend on the dataset's scaling.</p>
<ul class="ckm-facts"><li><b>Data:</b> <a href="../assets/learn/data/town_year.json" download>town_year.json</a> (8,760 hours of 2025), the course's year file: the real 2025 hourly demand, wind and solar of the Southwest Power Pool grid (EIA-930), each as a shape in thousandths of its own highest 2025 hour</li><li><b>Metadata:</b> the file's <code>meta</code> block gives the source, the time convention and how bad hours were filled</li><li><b>Scaling:</b> as lesson 0: demand × 450 MW, the wind farm × 150 MW, the solar farm × 200 MW, so SPP's highest hour means a farm at its full size</li><li><b>Compare:</b> each farm's output in the 100 hours of highest demand, and in the 100 hours of highest net load (demand minus wind and solar), with its average over the year</li><li><b>Ties:</b> where hours tie, take the earlier one first</li></ul>
<!-- ckm-brief-empirical:end -->
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-card ckm-supplied">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Part B · the supplied model, with one planted defect</p>
<!-- ckm-supplied:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p>The supplied model: what should Prairie Town build (wind, solar, a gas combined-cycle plant, a gas peaker) to meet demand on three representative days of 2025, each weighted by the days of the year it stands for? One planted defect.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">On paper</p><ul class="ckm-paper"><li><b>Weights:</b> <code>w_d = the days of the year that day d stands for (121, 122, 122; they sum to 365).</code></li><li><b>Goal:</b> <code>min Σ_g A_g K_g + Σ_d w_d Σ_t [ (Σ_g c_g p_g,d,t) + V u_d,t ]   ($ a year)</code></li><li><b>Balance:</b> <code>Σ_g p_g,d,t + u_d,t = D_d,t   (MW, every day and hour)</code></li><li><b>Wind and solar:</b> <code>p_g,d,t ≤ a_g,d,t K_g   (a: output per MW built, 0 to 1)</code></li><li><b>Gas plants:</b> <code>p_g,d,t ≤ K_g</code></li><li><b>Domains:</b> <code>K_g ≥ 0,  p_g,d,t ≥ 0,  u_d,t ≥ 0</code></li></ul>
<details class="lx-textalt ckm-sym"><summary>The symbols, with their units</summary><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Symbol</th><th scope="col">Meaning</th><th scope="col">Unit</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>g</code></td><td>a technology: wind, solar, gas combined-cycle (cc), gas peaker (pk)</td><td>–</td></tr><tr><td><code>d, t</code></td><td>a representative day, and an hour of it (t = 0 to 23, one hour each)</td><td>–</td></tr><tr><td><code>w_d</code></td><td>the days of the year that day d stands for</td><td>days</td></tr><tr><td><code>A_g</code></td><td>capital cost, already annualized</td><td>$ per MW of capacity per year</td></tr><tr><td><code>K_g</code></td><td>capacity built: a decision</td><td>MW</td></tr><tr><td><code>c_g</code></td><td>running cost</td><td>$/MWh</td></tr><tr><td><code>p_g,d,t</code></td><td>output in hour t of day d: a decision</td><td>MW (held for one hour, so also MWh)</td></tr><tr><td><code>u_d,t</code></td><td>demand left unserved: a decision</td><td>MW (also MWh in its hour)</td></tr><tr><td><code>V</code></td><td>the cost of unserved demand, $10,000</td><td>$/MWh</td></tr><tr><td><code>D_d,t</code></td><td>demand</td><td>MW</td></tr><tr><td><code>a_g,d,t</code></td><td>output per MW built, 0 to 1 (wind and solar)</td><td>MW per MW</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="lx-hint">Units of the goal: MW held for one hour × $/MWh = $ for each hour; summed over a day's 24 hours and multiplied by w_d days, $ a year, like A_g K_g.</p></details>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In code (the starter notebook runs it)</p><ol class="ckm-code"><li><span>DAYS = {&quot;winter&quot;: 121, &quot;shoulder&quot;: 122, &quot;summer&quot;: 122}       # days of 2025 each day stands for</span></li><li><span>weight = {d: DAYS[d] / 365 for d in DAYS}                    # share of the year</span></li><li><span>cost = {&quot;wind&quot;: 0, &quot;solar&quot;: 0, &quot;cc&quot;: 40, &quot;pk&quot;: 100}           # running cost, $ per MWh</span></li><li><span>capital = {&quot;wind&quot;: 100_000, &quot;solar&quot;: 70_000, &quot;cc&quot;: 80_000, &quot;pk&quot;: 50_000}   # $ per MW-year, annualized</span></li><li><span>V = 10_000                                                    # $ per MWh of demand left unserved</span></li><li><span>minimize( sum(capital[g] * K[g] for g) + sum(weight[d] * (sum(cost[g] * p[g,d,t] for g) + V * u[d,t]) for d, t) )</span></li><li><span>for d, t: sum(p[g,d,t] for g) + u[d,t] == demand[d][t]                 # balance, MW</span></li><li><span>for g in (&quot;wind&quot;, &quot;solar&quot;), d, t: p[g,d,t] &lt;= avail[g][d][t] * K[g]   # output per MW built</span></li><li><span>for g in (&quot;cc&quot;, &quot;pk&quot;), d, t: p[g,d,t] &lt;= K[g]</span></li><li><span>report(K, annual_cost=objective, demand_in_year=sum(weight[d] * demand[d][t] for d, t))</span></li></ol>
<ul class="ckm-facts ckm-notes"><li><b>Costs:</b> illustrative round numbers: capital already annualized ($ per MW of capacity per year); running costs as in lesson 0</li><li><b>Demand:</b> the three real days' SPP shape × 450 MW</li><li><b>Wind and solar:</b> output per MW built: the SPP shapes scaled to EIA's 2025 U.S. capacity factors (33.8% and 24.0%) with the course's scale method</li><li><b>Days:</b> Thursday 16 January 2025 for December to March (121 days); Wednesday 2 April 2025 for April, May, October and November (122 days); Monday 15 September 2025 for June to September (122 days)</li></ul>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>What the code prints when run</summary><table class="lx-facts ckm-report-t"><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Built: Wind farm</th><td class="n">0.0 MW</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Built: Solar farm</th><td class="n">0.0 MW</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Built: Gas combined-cycle</th><td class="n">0.0 MW</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Built: Gas peaker</th><td class="n">308.7 MW</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Annual cost</th><td class="n">$18.1 million</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Demand in the year</th><td class="n">6,757 MWh</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Demand left unserved in the year</th><td class="n">203 MWh</td></tr></tbody></table></details>
<!-- ckm-supplied:end -->

</div>

<div class="lx-fallback">

<ol class="ckm-static">
<li><p><b>Your formulation</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part A · Formulate</span></p><p>Write your formulation of the water brief: sets, parameters with units, decision variables, the objective and every rule. <li><p><b>Least cost of the day</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part A · Solve</span></p><p>Solve your model. What is the least electricity cost of the day, energy and demand charge together? Within 0.1% (about 50 cents) counts as right.</p><p>Answer with a number and a unit.</p></li>
<li><p><b>The highest draw</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part A · Read the solution</span></p><p>In your least-cost schedule, what is the pumps' highest hourly draw of electricity? Within 0.5% (about 1 kW) counts as right.</p><p>Answer with a number and a unit.</p></li>
<li><p><b>Water pumped at the peak price</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part A · Read the solution</span></p><p>How much water does your schedule pump in the five peak-price hours, 16:00 to 21:00? Within 1% (about 3 m³) counts as right.</p><p>Answer with a number and a unit.</p></li>
<li><p><b>A larger tower</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part A · Marginal value</span></p><p>Solve again with a tower 100 m³ larger (4,100 m³). By how much does the day's cost fall? Within 2% (about 14 cents) counts as right.</p><p>Answer with a number and a unit.</p></li>
<li><p><b>The planted defect</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part B · Find a defect</span></p><p>Run the supplied model (the button above, or the starter notebook) and read its code. Which line holds the planted defect?</p><ul><li>a. Line 2: weight = DAYS[d] / 365</li><li>b. Line 4: the annualized capital costs</li><li>c. Line 6: the objective</li><li>d. Line 8: the wind and solar limits</li></ul></li>
<li><p><b>The check that shows it</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part B · Find a defect</span></p><p>Which line of the supplied model's report shows the defect most directly?</p><ul><li>a. <li><p><b>The fixed model</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part B · Fix and re-solve</span></p><p>Fix the defect and solve again. What is the plan's annual cost? Within 0.5% (about $0.5 million) counts as right.</p><p>Answer with a number and a unit.</p></li>
<li><p><b>Upper bound by hand</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part C · Validate</span></p><p>Without the solver: what would the day cost if the pumps simply matched each hour's water use (pump as you go)? <li><p><b>Lower bound by hand</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part C · Validate</span></p><p>Without the solver: a lower bound, if every m³ could be pumped at the cheapest price and the draw spread evenly over the 24 hours. <li><p><b>Your validation statement</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part C · Validate and submit</span></p><p>State whether your optimum lies between your two bounds, one special case your model reproduces exactly, and what these checks cannot show. Submitting opens the worked solutions below.</p><p>Self-rated against 3 points, shown after you submit.</p></li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Empirical variant: the tasks</p>
<ol class="ckm-static">
<li><p><b>Your analysis design</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part A · Design the analysis</span></p><p>Write your design before computing: the question's type, the metrics with units, how you scale the data and pick the hours (with ties), and what the analysis leaves out.</p><p>Self-rated against 4 points, shown after you submit.</p></li>
<li><p><b>Wind's mean output in the dataset</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part A · Compute</span></p><p>In the dataset as scaled, what is the wind farm's mean output over 2025 as a percentage of its 150 MW, that is, of SPP's highest 2025 wind hour? Within 0.5% of the value (about 0.3 percentage points) counts as right.</p><p>Answer with a number and a unit.</p></li>
<li><p><b>Wind in the highest-demand hours</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part A · Compute</span></p><p>What is the wind farm's average output in the 100 hours of highest demand, as a share of its 150 MW? Within 2% of the value (about 1.2 percentage points) counts as right.</p><p>Answer with a number and a unit.</p></li>
<li><p><b>Solar in the highest-demand hours</b> <span class="lx-hint">Part A · Compute</span></p><p>And the solar farm's average output in the same 100 hours, as a share of its 200 MW? <header class="lx-x-head"><h3>Model variant: the water tower as a linear program</h3></header>
```

**Sets and inputs.** Hours $t = 0, \dots, 23$, each lasting $\Delta t = 1$ h. Water use $w_t$ (m³ in hour $t$); price $\pi_t$ (\$/kWh); $k = 0.5$ kWh/m³; pump limit $\bar Q = 900$ m³/h; tower limits $\underline S = 800$ and $\bar S = 4{,}000$ m³; start $S_0 = 2{,}000$ m³; demand charge $c = \$0.40$/kW.

**Decisions.** Water pumped $q_t$ (m³ in hour $t$), the tower's level at the end of each hour $s_t$ (m³), and the day's highest draw $P$ (kW).

$$\min \; \sum_t \pi_t\, k\, q_t \;+\; c\,P$$

$$s_t = s_{t-1} + q_t - w_t \;\;(s_{-1} = S_0), \qquad \underline S \le s_t \le \bar S,$$

$$0 \le q_t \le \bar Q\,\Delta t, \qquad P_t = k\,q_t / \Delta t \le P, \qquad s_{23} \ge S_0, \qquad P \ge 0 .$$

**Units.** $\pi_t k q_t$ is \$/kWh × kWh/m³ × m³ = \$; $cP$ is \$/kW × kW = \$. The hour's draw $P_t$ is its energy $k q_t$ (kWh) divided by $\Delta t = 1$ h, in kW; with $\Delta t = 1$ h the code's coefficients are the same numbers. The model has 49 variables, 24 tower rows, 24 draw rows and one end-of-day row. $P$ plays the part of a built capacity in M3: one number every hour must stay under, paid once.

```{=html}

<ol class="ckm-list"><li><b>Design first:</b> a descriptive screen; metrics in % of each farm's size and in MW; 100% means SPP's highest 2025 hour, so the year's mean is not a capacity factor; the top hours sorted from the highest, the earlier hour first on ties.</li><li><b>Load and check:</b> 8,760 hours, no gaps; demand peaks at 450 MW and totals 2,469 GWh; wind and solar never above their sizes; the time index is hour-ending, from the file's <code>start_utc</code>.</li><li><b>Compute:</b> averages over the year and over the two sets of 100 hours.</li></ol>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts ckm-sol"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Hours</th><th scope="col">Wind (% of 150 MW)</th><th scope="col">Solar (% of 200 MW)</th><th scope="col">Both (MW)</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>The whole year</td><td class="n">52.8%</td><td class="n">23.4%</td><td class="n">126.0</td></tr><tr><td>100 highest demand</td><td class="n">58.1%</td><td class="n">69.0%</td><td class="n">225.1</td></tr><tr><td>100 highest net load</td><td class="n">29.6%</td><td class="n">4.3%</td><td class="n">52.9</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<ul class="ckm-list"><li><b>At the demand peaks</b> (summer afternoons): both farms give more than their year averages.</li><li><b>At the net-load peaks</b> (evenings, winter nights and mornings): wind gives 0.56 of its average, and solar almost nothing. These are the hours the rest of the fleet must cover.</li><li><b>Against the benchmark:</b> the dataset's wind mean, 52.8% of its highest hour, is 19.0 percentage points above EIA's 2025 U.S. capacity factor of 33.8%; solar's 23.4% is close to EIA's 24.0%.</li><li><b>What the gap shows:</b> a definition difference (shares of the highest hour, not of capacity), plus SPP's own fleet and wind. These data cannot split the two, so the comparison checks a definition; it does not validate the numbers.</li><li><b>A like-for-like check</b> would divide SPP's 2025 wind output by its installed wind capacity: the same quantity, boundary and year as EIA's.</li><li><b>What survives, for the same hours:</b> rescaled linearly to 33.8% (each hour × 0.338 ÷ 0.5275), wind's MW and percentages fall by one factor, so its ratio to its own average in these 100 net-load hours stays 0.56.</li><li><b>If the hours are picked again</b> after rescaling, less wind raises net load in windy hours: 82 of the 100 hours stay, and the ratio becomes 0.71. Both are valid; say which you did.</li><li><b>What it leaves out:</b> one weather year, outages, imports and an <span class="lx-term" data-term="resource-adequacy">adequacy</span> model; averages over top hours screen, they do not measure a <span class="lx-term" data-term="capacity-credit">capacity credit</span>.</li></ul>

<!-- ckm-sol-defect:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<ol class="ckm-list"><li><b>Symptom:</b> a gas peaker only, demand left unserved, and a year that holds 6,757 MWh of demand: about one day of the town's.</li><li><b>Root cause, line 2:</b> <code>weight = DAYS[d] / 365</code> turns the days each representative day stands for into shares of the year. The paper says the weight is the number of days. With shares, the running costs of one average day meet a whole year of capital costs, so fuel looks almost free and capital-light plants win.</li><li><b>The check that shows it:</b> the year's total against an independent reference: the model's demand in the year, 6,757 MWh, against the town's 2,466 GWh. Units say the same: capital in $ a year, running costs in $ a day.</li><li><b>The fix:</b> <code>weight = DAYS</code> (121, 122, 122 days). Solve again.</li></ol>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts ckm-sol"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Report line</th><th scope="col">Supplied (defect)</th><th scope="col">Fixed</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Built: Wind farm</td><td class="n">0.0 MW</td><td class="n">548.4 MW</td></tr><tr><td>Built: Solar farm</td><td class="n">0.0 MW</td><td class="n">210.7 MW</td></tr><tr><td>Built: Gas combined-cycle</td><td class="n">0.0 MW</td><td class="n">151.9 MW</td></tr><tr><td>Built: Gas peaker</td><td class="n">308.7 MW</td><td class="n">54.3 MW</td></tr><tr><td>Annual cost</td><td class="n">$18.1 million</td><td class="n">$106.8 million</td></tr><tr><td>Demand in the year</td><td class="n">6,757 MWh</td><td class="n">2,466,275 MWh</td></tr><tr><td>Demand left unserved in the year</td><td class="n">203 MWh</td><td class="n">0 MWh</td></tr><tr><td>Cost per MWh of demand</td><td class="n">$2,682.20</td><td class="n">$43.31</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p class="lx-hint">The fixed plan is the answer to the model as written, not a recommendation: its costs are illustrative, and three typical days keep no extreme day, so the plan meets the peaks of those days, not the year's (M3 keeps the extremes).</p>
```
